title: Globalisation & the Future of Manufacture
description: How globalisation shapes manufacturing through international standards, employment, cost, sustainability and ethical.
content_html:
What Is Globalisation in Manufacturing?

Globalisation has fundamentally changed how products are made. A smartphone assembled in one country may contain a processor designed in the USA, memory chips from South Korea, a camera module from Japan, and a case moulded in China — all coordinated by a supply chain spanning dozens of countries. For engineering manufacturers, globalisation brings opportunities: access to lower-cost labour, specialist materials and larger markets. But it also introduces risks and responsibilities — around employment conditions, environmental impact, product quality standards and the ethics of international trade. Understanding globalisation's implications is an increasingly important part of the engineer's role.

International Standards

International standards are agreed specifications that allow manufacturers in different countries to produce components that are interchangeable, safe and of consistent quality. The most widely used system is the ISO (International Organisation for Standardisation) series. In engineering, standards govern dimensions (so an M10 bolt made in Germany will fit an M10 nut made in India), material properties, test methods, quality management systems (ISO 9001), and environmental management (ISO 14001). Without international standards, globalised manufacturing would be impossible — components from different countries would not fit together, and buyers could not rely on consistent quality from overseas suppliers.

For individual manufacturers, achieving ISO certification signals to customers that processes meet a recognised benchmark, opening access to international markets. Meeting standards also drives internal quality improvements. However, achieving and maintaining certification requires ongoing investment in auditing, documentation and process improvement.

Key Fact

International standards such as ISO 9001 (quality management) and ISO 14001 (environmental management) ensure that products made in different countries meet consistent quality and safety requirements. They enable interchangeable components, open access to global markets, and drive internal quality improvement — but require ongoing investment to achieve and maintain certification.

Influence on Employment Opportunities

Globalisation has profound and often controversial effects on employment. When a manufacturer moves production to a country with lower labour costs, jobs are lost in the country of origin — a process known as offshoring. UK manufacturing employment fell sharply in the 1980s and 1990s as industries relocated to countries where wages were a fraction of UK rates. This can devastate communities dependent on a single factory or industry.

However, globalisation also creates employment — in logistics, international trade, design, and the management of global supply chains. Higher-skill, higher-value roles may remain in the originating country while lower-skill production moves overseas. In the receiving country, factory jobs provide income and economic development, though the wages and conditions may be significantly below what would be acceptable in the manufacturer's home country. This raises ethical questions about whether companies have a responsibility to ensure fair wages and safe conditions throughout their supply chain.

Employment conditions vary enormously between countries. Minimum wage legislation, maximum working hours, health and safety regulations, and the right to organise trade unions differ widely. A product manufactured in a country with weaker regulations may be cheaper partly because workers receive lower pay, work longer hours in less safe conditions, and have fewer rights than workers in the country where the product is sold. Consumers and companies face an ethical choice: prioritise lower product costs, or insist on supply chain standards that protect workers regardless of location. Initiatives such as ethical trade accreditation and supply chain auditing aim to address this imbalance.

Product Cost, Transportation and Sustainability

Globalisation affects product cost in complex ways. Lower overseas labour costs reduce manufacturing cost, but the requirement for transportation — shipping, air freight, and road haulage across international supply chains — adds logistics cost, lead time and carbon emissions. Just-in-time supply chains that depend on rapid international freight are particularly vulnerable to disruptions such as port congestion, fuel price spikes or geopolitical events. The 2021 global shipping container shortage significantly increased manufacturing costs and delayed production across many industries.

The sustainability implications of globalised manufacturing are significant. Long-distance freight generates substantial carbon emissions — particularly air freight, which emits around 50 times more CO₂ per tonne-kilometre than sea freight. This conflicts with manufacturers' sustainability targets and national carbon-reduction commitments. Reshoring (bringing production closer to the end market) and nearshoring (moving production to nearby countries rather than distant ones) are strategies companies use to reduce transportation emissions, shorten supply chains and improve resilience.

Key Fact

Globalisation reduces manufacturing unit cost through lower overseas labour, but increases transportation cost, carbon emissions and supply chain risk. Air freight emits approximately 50 times more CO₂ per tonne-kilometre than sea freight. Reshoring and nearshoring are strategies to reduce transportation impact and improve supply chain resilience.

Economic: lower production costs benefit consumers through cheaper products and companies through higher margins, but risk deindustrialisation of high-wage economies and dependency on foreign suppliers for critical goods. Social: job losses in manufacturing communities can cause long-term unemployment and social decline; but global employment growth in developing countries has lifted millions out of poverty. Ethical: consumers in wealthy countries benefit from low prices partly achieved through low wages and poor conditions elsewhere — companies have a responsibility to audit their supply chains. Environmental: long supply chains increase carbon emissions; manufacturing in countries with weaker environmental regulation may involve practices (pollution, waste disposal) that would be illegal at home. These four dimensions always need to be considered together when evaluating any globalisation decision.
exam_tip_html: For evaluate questions on globalisation, structure your answer across all four dimensions: economic (cost, employment, market access), social (job losses, community impact, development in receiving countries), ethical (supply chain conditions, fair wages), and environmental (transportation emissions, weaker regulations overseas). A top-band answer will not just list these — it will weigh them against each other and reach a substantiated judgement. For ISO standards questions, name specific examples: ISO 9001 for quality management, ISO 14001 for environmental management. When discussing transportation, always link it to both cost and carbon emissions — the exam expects both.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • International standards such as ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 enable globalised manufacture by ensuring consistent quality and interchangeable components, while opening access to international markets — but require ongoing investment to achieve and maintain.
  • Globalisation reduces manufacturing cost through lower overseas labour but increases transportation cost and carbon emissions, and raises ethical questions about employment conditions and supply chain responsibility.
  • Evaluating globalisation requires considering economic, social, ethical and environmental implications together — and companies must weigh cost advantages against supply chain resilience, sustainability targets and their responsibility to workers throughout the supply chain.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which manufacturing, trade and business have become increasingly interconnected across national borders, with companies sourcing, producing and selling worldwide.
Agreed technical specifications, such as ISO standards, that ensure products meet consistent quality, safety and interoperability requirements regardless of where they are manufactured.
The environmental, social and economic impact of transporting goods over long distances as part of a global supply chain, including carbon emissions, energy use and dependency on fossil fuels.
The practice of relocating manufacturing or business processes to a country with lower costs, typically resulting in job losses in the originating country.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best explains why international standards are important in globalised manufacturing?
A) They allow each country to set its own unique product dimensions
B) They ensure components made in different countries are interchangeable and meet consistent quality requirements
C) They prevent manufacturers from moving production to lower-cost countries
D) They require all manufacturers to use the same machinery and production methods
practice_questions.marks: B) They ensure components made in different countries are interchangeable and meet consistent quality requirements [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two implications of globalisation for employment in the UK manufacturing industry.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: job losses in manufacturing as production moves to lower-cost countries (offshoring) / loss of lower-skill production roles while higher-skill design and management roles may remain / communities dependent on single industries can be severely affected / new employment created in logistics, supply chain management and international trade. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the transportation required by global supply chains has implications for sustainability.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that long-distance freight generates carbon emissions. Second mark: air freight in particular emits approximately 50 times more CO₂ per tonne-kilometre than sea freight, making it particularly damaging. Third mark: this conflicts with manufacturers' sustainability targets and national carbon-reduction commitments, particularly when products could be manufactured closer to the end market (reshoring/nearshoring). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what ISO 9001 is and give one benefit to a manufacturing company of achieving ISO 9001 certification.
practice_questions.marks: Description (2 marks): ISO 9001 is an international standard that specifies the requirements for a quality management system — it sets out how a company should control its processes to ensure products consistently meet customer and regulatory requirements (2 marks for a developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'it is a quality standard'). Benefit (2 marks): a company with ISO 9001 certification signals to international customers that its processes meet a recognised global benchmark, opening access to overseas contracts that require certified suppliers — without it the company may be excluded from bidding (2 marks for a specific, developed benefit; 1 mark for a vague answer). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A UK manufacturer of industrial components is considering moving its production to a lower-cost country to reduce manufacturing costs. However, the company has recently committed to a carbon-reduction target.

Discuss the economic and environmental factors the company should consider before making this decision.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering economic factors (lower labour costs in the target country would reduce unit manufacturing cost, potentially improving competitiveness or margins; however, logistics and shipping costs must be added, and supply chain disruption risk increases), and environmental factors (longer supply chain means greater freight emissions, likely by sea but possibly air for urgent orders; manufacturing in a country with weaker environmental regulations may also involve production practices that increase the company's overall environmental footprint; both conflict with the carbon-reduction commitment). Both dimensions developed and linked to the scenario, with some acknowledgement of the tension between them.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two relevant factors identified, briefly explained, some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One factor from each dimension but not developed.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
An international consumer electronics company sources components from manufacturers across Asia, Europe and South America. A recent investigation revealed that some suppliers use excessive working hours and pay below the living wage in their countries.

Evaluate the extent to which a company has a responsibility to ensure ethical employment conditions throughout its global supply chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that constructs the argument for responsibility (consumers buy the final product believing the company endorses all aspects of its production; the company profits from lower costs partly achieved through poor conditions; reputational and legal risks — supply chain transparency legislation (e.g. UK Modern Slavery Act) means companies can be held accountable; the company has leverage to demand standards as a major customer). Then challenges this: the company cannot directly control independent suppliers in other countries; different legal frameworks mean what is legal abroad may be unacceptable at home; the cost of supply chain auditing is significant; forcing higher wages may make the supply uneconomic and shift production to less-auditable suppliers. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached — e.g. the company has both a moral and legal responsibility, but must act through specific enforceable supplier codes of conduct, regular auditing and willingness to exit relationships with non-compliant suppliers, rather than assuming responsibility can be delegated.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to the scenario and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development or evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which ISO standard relates specifically to quality management systems?
Which of the following is a key sustainability disadvantage of global supply chains compared to local manufacture?
options: Greater transportation carbon emissions from long-distance freight
Inability to meet international quality standards

knowledge_checks.q: Moving production from a high-wage country to a lower-cost country is known as _____, a practice that often leads to job losses in the originating country.
Air freight emits approximately _____ times more CO₂ per tonne-kilometre than sea freight, making it the most carbon-intensive mode of international logistics.
Match each globalisation implication to its correct category.
left: Job losses in UK manufacturing communities
Suppliers paying below living wage overseas
right: Ethical implication — responsibility for supply chain working conditions
Social implication — impact on communities and employment
Environmental implication — sustainability of global logistics

flashcard_questions.q: What is globalisation in the context of manufacturing?
flashcard_questions.a: Globalisation is the process by which manufacturing and trade have become interconnected across borders, with companies sourcing, producing and selling worldwide.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are international standards important in globalised manufacturing?
flashcard_questions.a: International standards ensure components made in different countries are interchangeable and meet consistent quality requirements, making global supply chains possible.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two ISO standards relevant to engineering manufacture and state what each covers.
flashcard_questions.a: ISO 9001 covers quality management systems; ISO 14001 covers environmental management systems — both are internationally recognised benchmarks for business processes.

flashcard_questions.q: What is offshoring and what is its main economic driver?
flashcard_questions.a: Offshoring is relocating production to a lower-cost country; the main driver is reducing manufacturing cost through lower labour wages in the destination country.

flashcard_questions.q: State one social consequence of offshoring for communities in the originating country.
flashcard_questions.a: Offshoring causes job losses in manufacturing communities that can lead to long-term unemployment and social decline, particularly in areas dependent on a single industry.

flashcard_questions.q: How does transportation in global supply chains affect sustainability?
flashcard_questions.a: Long-distance freight generates significant carbon emissions — air freight emits around 50 times more CO₂ per tonne-kilometre than sea freight — conflicting with carbon-reduction targets.

flashcard_questions.q: What is reshoring and why are companies increasingly considering it?
flashcard_questions.a: Reshoring means bringing production back closer to the end market; companies do it to reduce transportation emissions, shorten supply chains and improve resilience to disruption.

flashcard_questions.q: State one ethical implication of globalised manufacturing for companies.
flashcard_questions.a: Companies have a responsibility to ensure workers throughout their global supply chain receive fair wages and work in safe conditions, even when operating under different national laws.

flashcard_questions.q: How does globalisation affect product cost for consumers?
flashcard_questions.a: Globalisation generally reduces product cost to consumers through lower overseas labour costs, though logistics and supply chain risks can partially offset these savings.

flashcard_questions.q: State one economic advantage and one economic disadvantage of globalisation for a UK manufacturer.
flashcard_questions.a: Advantage: access to lower-cost overseas production reduces unit manufacturing cost; disadvantage: dependence on overseas suppliers creates vulnerability to supply chain disruptions.

flashcard_questions.q: What does ISO 14001 cover and why is it relevant to globalised manufacture?
flashcard_questions.a: ISO 14001 covers environmental management systems; it helps companies demonstrate sustainability commitments to international customers and regulators across global supply chains.

flashcard_questions.q: State the four dimensions that should be considered when evaluating the implications of globalisation.
flashcard_questions.a: The four dimensions are economic (cost and employment), social (community impact), ethical (supply chain conditions) and environmental (carbon emissions and regulations).
